question: What are the structural safety assessment and access restriction protocols following earthquake damage in a volcanic-seismic crisis?
answer: Per OASP post-earthquake rapid assessment procedures (EMS-98) and Hellenic Ministry of Infrastructure guidelines: (1) RAPID VISUAL SCREENING (RVS): Trained engineers conduct drive-by or walk-by inspection of all structures — classify as Green (inspected/safe), Yellow (restricted use), Red (unsafe/do not enter) using FEMA P-154 methodology; (2) INSPECTION PRIORITY: P1=public buildings (hospitals, schools, EOC), P2=critical infrastructure (ports, airports, utilities), P3=hotels and tourist accommodation, P4=residential; (3) CALDERA RIM AREAS: Enhanced monitoring of caldera cliff stability — any new crack formation (>5cm width) or ground settlement triggers immediate Red exclusion zone for that section; coordinate with EKPA geotechnical engineers; (4) OLD/TRADITIONAL BUILDINGS: All pre-1960 unreinforced masonry buildings in affected area automatically restricted until inspected — post-1985 seismically designed RC structures assessed individually; (5) AFTERSHOCK PROTOCOL: After any M≥4.5 aftershock — all Yellow-rated buildings re-inspected before re-entry; all Red exclusion zones maintained; (6) TEMPORARY HOUSING: Red-rated residents directed to pre-designated reception centers (sports halls, hotel complexes in unaffected areas); (7) UTILITY DISCONNECTION: DEDDIE (Greek electricity distributor) disconnects power to all Red-rated buildings; EYDAP water supply checked for damage in affected zones; (8) RE-INSPECTION: Yellow buildings re-assessed after 72 hours of reduced seismicity (<M3.5).

question: What is the aerial firefighting coordination protocol for managing air tankers and helicopters over an active wildfire?
answer: Per NWCG Airspace Coordination procedures (PMS 515) and USFS Aviation Procedures Manual: (1) AIR TACTICAL GROUP SUPERVISOR (ATGS): All aerial operations are supervised by the ATGS ('Air Attack') flying overhead — ATGS has authority over all aircraft in the Fire Traffic Area (FTA); no aircraft enters FTA without ATGS authorization; (2) FIRE TRAFFIC AREA (FTA): Established immediately upon aviation deployment — extends 5nm radius, surface to 3,000ft AGL (or as designated); all aircraft report to designated air-to-ground frequency on entry; (3) AIRCRAFT SEPARATION: Minimum 500ft vertical separation between fixed-wing and rotary-wing; airtankers make drops at <150 knots to minimize retardant scatter; helicopters operate in designated altitude bands (below 1,500ft); (4) DROP COORDINATION: ATGS directs each drop via radio — specifies target, approach heading, and retardant coverage level (CL-1 to CL-5); Leadplane leads first airtanker drop in unfamiliar terrain; (5) SAFETY: Crew-carrying helicopters must be grounded before airtanker makes drop in same sector; no drops within 300ft of ground personnel without explicit ground unit approval; (6) NIGHT OPERATIONS: Fixed-wing airtankers grounded 30 minutes after sunset unless Night Air Attack (NAAS) certified; FLIR-equipped helicopters may continue with ATGS coordination; (7) PILOT WEATHER MINIMUMS: Fixed-wing — 500ft ceiling, 1 mile visibility; helicopters — 300ft ceiling, 0.5 mile; suspend all operations below minimums.

question: What is the structure defense and wildland-urban interface (WUI) protocol when wildfire threatens residential areas?
answer: Per NFPA 1144, NFPA 1 Chapter 38 (WUI), and Hellenic Fire Service WUI guidance: (1) THREAT ASSESSMENT: Evaluate structure ignitability — assess 0-30ft zone (immediate zone: remove combustibles, propane, wood piles from structure), 30-100ft zone (intermediate: reduce fuel density, create defensible space), 100-200ft zone (outer: reduce fuel continuity); (2) STRUCTURE TRIAGE: With limited resources, apply LCES and triage structures: SAVE (defensible, prepared, low-slope terrain), MONITOR (partially prepared, assess during attack), LEAVE (unprepared, poor access/egress, high-fuel density, indefensible); (3) PREPARATION: For SAVE structures — close all windows/vents, remove patio furniture/doormats, connect garden hoses and fill any pools/tanks, shut off gas at meter, leave lights on for visibility in smoke; (4) STRUCTURE DEFENSE TACTICS: Engine crew at structure — use foam or water to wet combustibles in 0-30ft zone; protect eaves, vents, and wooden decks (primary ignition points); never allow crew to be surrounded by fire without safe exit; (5) EGRESS: Every crew must have two identified escape routes and safety zone; pull out if fire reaches property line with <5 minutes remaining; (6) BURNOVER: If entrapped — deploy fire shelter in pre-cleared area, never in drainage or chimney terrain; (7) POST-FIRE: Patrol for hot spots, re-ignition from retained ember loads in wood structural members.

question: What is the overnight operational period protocol for managing a large wildfire from dusk to dawn?
answer: Per NWCG Incident Management principles and ICS Operational Period Briefing procedures: (1) OPERATIONAL PERIOD TRANSITION: Outgoing Operations Section Chief briefs incoming night OSC at 1800 using ICS 204 Assignment Lists — covers current fire perimeter, suppression objectives, active threats, crew positions, and pending resource arrivals; (2) NIGHT FIRE BEHAVIOR: Generally lower ROS (Rate of Spread) due to higher relative humidity and lower temperatures — use night hours for: firing operations (burnout along fireline), structure prep (WUI), direct attack on weakened flanks, and fireline construction in safer sectors; (3) AVIATION: Fixed-wing tankers grounded at sunset (unless NAAS); FLIR helicopters continue night reconnaissance — report hot spots to OSC every hour; (4) CREW SAFETY: All crews must remain on assigned sectors — no cross-sector movement without OSC approval; vehicle lights required on all roads; 2-hour rest (8-hour off) minimum per NWCG work/rest ratio policy; (5) WEATHER: Night weather observation every 2 hours from assigned FBAN (Fire Behavior Analyst) — alert OSC of any humidity recovery failure (<50% RH by 0300 indicates dangerous morning conditions); (6) MORNING TRANSITION: Full Operational Period Briefing at 0600 — incorporate overnight FBAN spot forecast for diurnal wind shift timing; pre-position airtankers for early morning window; (7) DAWN PATROL: Aviation reconnaissance of entire perimeter at first light to identify overnight escapes before full crew deployment.

question: What is the specific emergency response protocol for a large-scale anhydrous ammonia (NH3) industrial release per NIOSH and NRT guidance?
answer: Per NIOSH Emergency Response Card for Ammonia (UN 1005) and NRT Anhydrous Ammonia Quick Reference Guide: PROPERTIES: Ammonia (NH3) — colorless gas, pungent odor detectable at 5 ppm; IDLH = 300 ppm; ERPG-2 = 150 ppm (1 hour); ERPG-3 = 750 ppm. Heavier than air at low temperatures, lighter above 15°C — check ambient temperature; (1) PPE: Level A (pressure-demand SCBA + fully encapsulating suit) for hot zone; Level B downwind in warm zone; Level C (ammonia-specific APF >25 cartridge) only when concentration confirmed <50 ppm; (2) ISOLATION: Initial isolation radius 100m all directions; protective action distance downwind depends on release size — for large spill (>1 ton), protective action distances extend to 1.1 km downwind in day, 4.4 km at night (cooler air, worse dispersion); (3) DECONTAMINATION: Emergency decon — copious water flush for minimum 15 minutes; remove ALL contaminated clothing; ammonia is highly water-soluble (flush is effective); (4) MEDICAL: Respiratory: 100% O2 immediately; bronchospasm — nebulized bronchodilator (salbutamol); pulmonary edema may be delayed 24 hours — ALL exposed persons observed minimum 12 hours; Eye: irrigate continuously with normal saline for minimum 30 minutes; (5) FIRE: Ammonia is flammable at 15–28% concentration — LEL = 15%; avoid sparks; use fog water to knock down vapors; (6) LEAK CONTROL: Only HAZMAT-trained personnel with Level A PPE may approach leak source; use water spray to disperse ammonia vapors but avoid directing at liquid ammonia (aerosol risk).
resources_required: Level A/B PPE, SCBA, ammonia-specific gas monitors (electrochemical), decon corridor, medical team, nebulized bronchodilators, ophthalmology support

question: What is the CBRN mass decontamination corridor protocol for large numbers of potentially contaminated civilians?
answer: Per NATO STANAG 2083 CBRN doctrine and CDC CHEMPACK Mass Casualty Decontamination guidelines: TRIGGER: Mass decontamination is activated when >10 symptomatic or potentially contaminated civilians present simultaneously. (1) SITE SELECTION: Establish decontamination corridor: upwind and uphill of contamination zone, accessible by ambulances, minimum 150m from release point, large open space for throughput; (2) CORRIDOR STRUCTURE: Lane 1 (ambulatory): Self-undress tent → dry decon (brush-off solids) → wet decon (emergency shower, cold/warm water) → towel dry → disposable clothing → medical triage exit; Lane 2 (non-ambulatory): Stretcher-carried through same stages with medic support; (3) THROUGHPUT: Each lane targets 200 persons/hour minimum; staffing ratio = 1 trained decon staff : 10 persons; (4) WATER MANAGEMENT: Collect runoff to prevent environmental contamination — berm decon area, pump to holding tank for disposal per EPA RCRA; (5) PPE: Decon staff in Level B minimum; Level A for non-ambulatory lane if substance unidentified; (6) SECONDARY CONTAMINATION PREVENTION: Victims' clothing and personal effects double-bagged and labeled; restrict exit from decon until cleared by HAZMAT assessment; (7) MEDICAL TRIAGE: Medical officer at exit triage — S1 (immediate), S2 (delayed), S3 (minor), S4 (expectant); administer antidotes at triage (atropine/2-PAM for organophosphate, hydroxocobalamin for cyanide); (8) DOCUMENTATION: Photo ID and medical record for each person through decon.

question: What is the crush syndrome and traumatic arrest protocol for victims extracted from collapsed buildings or prolonged entrapment?
answer: Per ATACC (Advanced Trauma Care for Combat) and WHO Earthquake Medical Response guidelines: Crush syndrome (rhabdomyolysis) occurs when compressive force is released after >1 hour entrapment — released myoglobin causes acute renal failure and cardiac arrhythmia. (1) PRE-EXTRICATION FLUID LOADING: Begin IV normal saline 1 litre/hour BEFORE releasing compression — target minimum 1 litre infused before extrication; (2) MONITORING: Attach cardiac monitor before extrication — potassium release on decompression can cause immediate VF/VT; have defibrillator ready; (3) FIELD TOURNIQUET: Apply tourniquet to crushed limb 5 minutes before release if amputation is planned or limb is non-viable — reduces systemic toxin load; (4) POST-EXTRICATION FLUID RESUSCITATION: Target urine output 200-300 mL/hour (vs. normal 50 mL/hr) — aggressive fluid loading; urinary catheter mandatory; (5) ALKALINIZATION: Sodium bicarbonate IV (1 mEq/kg) to alkalinize urine — prevents myoglobin precipitation in renal tubules; (6) HYPERKALEMIA: Treat potassium >6.0 mEq/L with: IV calcium gluconate (cardiac membrane stabilization), insulin + glucose (drive K into cells), salbutamol nebulization; (7) HOSPITAL: All crush syndrome patients require ICU — anticipate dialysis within 24-72 hours; avoid NSAIDs and nephrotoxic agents; (8) TRIAGE: In MCI setting — crush syndrome patients are S2 (delayed) if haemodynamically stable but require definitive hospital care urgently.

question: What is the WHO IHR 2005 protocol for declaring and responding to a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC)?
answer: Per WHO International Health Regulations (2005) and WHO Pandemic Influenza Risk Management guidance: (1) NATIONAL NOTIFICATION: Under IHR Article 6, States Parties must notify WHO within 24 hours of assessing an event that may constitute a PHEIC using the Decision Instrument (Annex 2) — based on: impact severity, unusual/unexpected nature, potential for international spread, and risk of travel/trade restrictions; (2) WHO ASSESSMENT: WHO Director-General convenes Emergency Committee of international experts to assess PHEIC criteria — committee may request additional information from affected state; (3) PHEIC DECLARATION: If DG declares PHEIC, issues Temporary Recommendations to all States Parties — may include: travel/trade measures, health measures at points of entry, surveillance requirements; (4) NATIONAL RESPONSE ACTIVATION: PHEIC triggers national pandemic plan activation (Greece: ΕΟΔΥ/EODY National Pandemic Plan): (a) Activate Health Emergency Operations Centre (HEOC); (b) Surge healthcare capacity — postpone elective procedures, discharge stable patients; (c) Activate PPE stockpiles and pre-pandemic antiviral reserves; (d) Initiate contact tracing for initial cases; (5) RISK COMMUNICATION: WHO issues public risk communication within 24 hours of PHEIC — coordinated national messaging to prevent panic/misinformation; (6) INTERNATIONAL COORDINATION: IHR Emergency Committee issues recommendations on laboratory sharing, vaccine development, and case definitions — all WHO Member States report case data weekly.

question: What is the hospital surge capacity protocol for managing a mass influx of infectious disease patients during a pandemic?
answer: Per WHO Hospital Preparedness Checklist for Pandemics and CDC Healthcare Coalition Surge guidance: SURGE LEVELS — Level 1 (Conventional): routine operations within existing capacity; Level 2 (Contingency): crisis standards implemented, non-critical services postponed; Level 3 (Crisis): standards of care altered, scarce resource allocation protocols activated. (1) SPACE SURGE: Convert non-clinical areas to patient care: conference rooms, cafeterias, parking structures — pre-identify conversion plans with engineering support; establish field hospitals in liaison with military or civil protection; (2) STAFF SURGE: Recall retired staff; cross-train non-critical care nurses for respiratory support; waive non-essential regulatory barriers (as per national emergency authority); establish staggered shift patterns to limit cross-exposure; (3) SUPPLY SURGE: Activate emergency procurement (PPE, ventilators, O2 supply, antiviral medications); join national/regional consortium purchasing; (4) COHORTING: Cohort infectious patients by pathogen/stage — separate confirmed, suspected, and clean zones with directional airflow where possible; (5) TRIAGE PROTOCOL: Implement mSTaRT or similar triage sieve for infectious disease severity — priority for ventilator allocation in Crisis Level per SOFA score or validated triage tool; (6) DISCHARGE: Accelerate discharge of stable patients to community care — activate home monitoring (pulse oximetry, remote check-in) for lower-acuity cases; (7) STAFF PROTECTION: N95/FFP2 for all respiratory care; powered air-purifying respirator (PAPR) for aerosol-generating procedures; test-to-return protocol for exposed staff.

question: What is the law enforcement protocol for managing large-scale civil unrest and public disorder during or after a major disaster?
answer: Per Hellenic Police civil unrest protocols and NIMS law enforcement integration guidelines: (1) INTELLIGENCE: Gather real-time intelligence on crowd size, mood, flashpoints, and organizer contacts — assign plain-clothes liaison officers to protest areas; brief Police Silver Tactical Commander every 30 minutes; (2) COMMUNICATION FIRST: Designated Liaison Officer makes immediate verbal contact with crowd leaders — communicate police intent, offer dialogue, explain safety boundaries; this step is mandatory before any physical measures; (3) GRADUATED RESPONSE (MOAB): Management → Open display of numbers → Actions → Back to safety: Stage 1 (M): dialogue and negotiation; Stage 2 (O): visible police presence in full protective equipment; Stage 3 (A): targeted arrest of instigators; Stage 4: retreat to safety lines if violence escalates beyond control; (4) MUTUAL AID: Request reinforcements when crowd >police ratio exceeds 15:1 — coordinate through GOLD commander for regional deployment; (5) USE OF FORCE CONTINUUM: Verbal commands → Physical presence → Soft empty-hand control → Hard empty-hand control → Less-lethal (water cannon, CS, rubber baton rounds) → Lethal force only when life threatened; all use-of-force justified, proportionate, and documented immediately; (6) MEDIA: Designate media liaison — pre-brief accredited journalists on safety zones; prevent unauthorized filming of police tactical positions; (7) ARRESTS: Field Processing Units established at outer perimeter — process, medically screen, and transport arrestees within 4 hours; (8) POST-INCIDENT: Full review within 48 hours — document all use-of-force incidents for accountability.

question: What is the protocol for managing looting, anti-social behaviour, and security enforcement in a post-disaster environment?
answer: Per NIMS law enforcement integration and post-disaster security guidelines: (1) LEGAL FRAMEWORK: Confirm declaration of state of emergency which may grant additional law enforcement powers — consult with legal counsel before implementing enhanced enforcement measures; (2) PRIORITY CRIME PREVENTION: P1 = violent crimes, looting in progress; P2 = property crime, burglary of disaster-affected premises; P3 = curfew/access zone violations; maintain proportionality — disaster victims who take food/water in survival context should not be criminally charged; (3) PATROL STRATEGY: Rolling vehicle patrols in evacuated zones every 30 minutes; foot patrols in densely populated shelter areas; static posts at critical facilities (hospitals, fuel depots, pharmacies, ATMs); (4) CURFEW ENFORCEMENT: Issue curfew via official government channels (WEA/EAS) — post multilingual signage at all entry points; first encounter = warning and identity check; repeat = citation or arrest; (5) COMMUNITY LIAISON: Establish police community liaison at each major shelter — take crime reports, address community concerns, build trust to encourage self-policing; (6) INTELLIGENCE: Coordinate with fire and utility crews working in affected areas — they observe suspicious activity and report to police; (7) DOCUMENTATION: All patrol encounters documented — supports post-disaster criminal prosecutions; photograph all looted premises for insurance and prosecution; (8) MUTUAL AID: Augment local police with Hellenic Police rapid deployment units and National Guard if needed.

question: What is the helicopter search and rescue (HEMS) protocol for evacuating injured victims from remote or inaccessible terrain?
answer: Per EASA HEMS operations rules (EU 965/2012) and Hellenic Air Force/Coast Guard SAR helicopter procedures: (1) MISSION AUTHORIZATION: Helicopter Emergency Medical Service (HEMS) activation requires: patient requiring urgent care, ground access impossible or too slow, adequate landing zone (LZ) available or hoisting conditions acceptable; (2) LZ SELECTION: Clear area minimum 30×30m; slope <10°; clear approach path 150m minimum; surface suitable for helicopter skids (grass, compacted soil); mark LZ centre with H in high-contrast colour; signal with smoke grenade (smoke deployed 30 seconds before helicopter arrival, deployed upwind); (3) LZ SAFETY: Ground crews face away from landing helicopter; remove all loose material (dust, leaves, tarps); bystanders minimum 60m from LZ; (4) HOIST OPERATIONS: When LZ impossible — patient secured in rescue harness or basket; helicopter approaches to hover 50–70m above victim; paramedic lowered via hoist; victim packaged and raised (max 250 kg total including paramedic); (5) NIGHT HOIST: FLIR/NVG equipped helicopter required; mark victim location with infrared strobe (visible to NVG but not visible to eye); (6) HANDOVER: Helicopter paramedic completes verbal handover to receiving emergency department: mechanism of injury, vital signs trends, interventions, allergies, medications; (7) SAFETY: Never approach helicopter from rear (tail rotor); always approach from front in full view of pilot; ducking mandatory under low main rotor.

question: What is the emergency supply chain and mutual aid resource mobilization protocol under NIMS/ICS?
answer: Per FEMA NIMS Resource Management doctrine and Emergency Management Assistance Compact (EMAC) procedures: (1) RESOURCE REQUEST: All resource requests submitted via ICS 213RR (Resource Request Message) through the Logistics Section — no direct field-to-field requests; specifies: resource type, quantity, reporting location, date/time needed, estimated duration, ordering unit contact; (2) LOCAL FIRST: Exhaust local resources before requesting mutual aid — check county and regional caches; (3) INTRASTATE MUTUAL AID: Submit request to State Emergency Management Agency (GSCP in Greece) via EMVOLOS system — state coordinates deployment from nearest available source; (4) INTERSTATE/INTERNATIONAL MUTUAL AID: Request through EMAC (US) or EU Civil Protection Mechanism (EU) for cross-border resources — 24–48 hour delivery timeline; (5) CREDENTIALING: All incoming mutual aid resources must be credentialed before deployment — verify training, experience, and equipment certification; deploy to appropriate position per competence; (6) DEMOBILIZATION: Plan demobilization from incident start — track all resources with expected release date; notify home jurisdiction 24 hours before demobilization; complete all paperwork before departure; (7) COST DOCUMENTATION: Track all expenditures with receipts, timesheets, and equipment usage logs from day one — required for FEMA disaster declaration reimbursement or EU Solidarity Fund claims; (8) REIMBURSEMENT TIMELINE: Compile cost documentation within 30 days for preliminary submission; final audit within 90 days.
